excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<kevaundray> With this decision, it depends on where we want to put the complexity.

If the cryptography code takes in multiple SRSs, then it will need to handle running them in parallel also. It may also mean that the cryptography code _could_ return null, if the javascript code gave it the same randomness.

If we call the cryptography code multiple times, then the javascript code will update the different SRSs in parallel, by running each wasm call in parallel, the js code would also be responsible for ensuring that they used different randomness. If the same randomness is used and not checked for, it would be rejected by the co-ordinator instead

<dankrad> > <dankrad>  we don't need it to stop on same randomness. discussed this with Carl already: if people want to cheat, they just publish their randomness or save it for later. same randomness is an unimportant edge case of defecting (re @kevaundray: With this decision, it depends on where we want to put the complexity.

If the cryptography code takes in multiple SRSs, then it will need to handle running them in parallel also. It may also mean that the cryptography code _could_ return null, if the javascript code gave it the same randomness.

If we call the cryptography code multiple times, then the javascript code will update the different SRSs in parallel, by running each wasm call in parallel, the js code would also be responsible for ensuring that they used different randomness. If the same randomness is used and not checked for, it would be rejected by the co-ordinator instead)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<dankrad> Yeah I don't like these kind of checks. I think they just fool you into believing you have increased resilience but don't add anything.

E.g. if your secrets are 1*s, 2*s and 3*s it's just as bad as s, s, s, but the check doesn't know anything about it

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <dankrad> > <dankrad>  I think the reason you sometimes get it as a file that you need to destroy is that some ceremonies are multi-round. For a single-round ceremony the secret should only ever be in memory, saving it to a disk would really be purely detrimental (you can delete that file but it is still only a copy of what you have in memory) (re @CarlBeek: imo the waste isn't something the user should have access to ever. i think it is a silly concept to give someone a file and tell them it needs to be destroyed. you either trust your contribution system or not. (and you're welcome to add airgaps etc to increase that trust))
